https://www.crash.net/f1/news/1101972/1/.text: George Russell, Mercedes F1 Team, 2026 Hungarian GP © XPB Images Prefer Crash.Net on Google See our stories more often Add Mercedes has shed more light on the issue that led to George Russell’s car going into anti-stall and wrecking his Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix. The Briton plummeted from sixth on the grid to the back of the pack as he struggled to get off the line. It later emerged that he’d gone into anti-stall, forcing him into a recovery driver that saw him eventually finish seventh. Russell is set to start seventh in Hungary Mercedes ’ Deputy team principal Bradley Lord explained in the squad’s post-race debrief that George Russell was “under 10% of throttle” at lights out as he tried to manage a rev spike. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “As the drivers wait for the start, they hold what are called their wait revs, which is holding the engine’s RPM at a specific level,” Lord said. “As George was doing that, the revs actually rose out of proportion to what he was asking for from the throttle. “The revs hit the rev limiter at the maximum RPM that the engine allows at that point, and then George tried to get it back under control to optimise and control his start. “He wasn't able to do so, and as he was lifting right off the throttle to under 10% of throttle demand, the lights went out. Read Also Mercedes cautious of "more intense" title threat ahead of F1 resumption George Russell breaks summer silence with personal announcement “And so he made a start with effectively much too little throttle through no fault of his own. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “That meant the anti-stall kicked in so he dropped to the back of the field.” It continued a wretched run to the summer break for the 28-year-old, who retired on the opening lap of the Belgian Grand Prix after contact with Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton. Lord praised Russell’s recovery drive, and believes he could have been higher up the field had the virtual safety car for a stricken Oscar Piastri been timed better. Russell was once again struck by misfortune “From there it was an incredible recovery drive,” he added. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “He picked the cars in front of him off one-by-one as he went through that first stint and actually was also unlucky with the timing of the virtual safety car at the end of the race. “It came out one lap after his second stop. “Had he been able to take advantage of it and get a free stop as such under the VSC, he could have finished even higher up than his eventual P7 finishing position.” Russell is now 59 points shy of Mercedes team-mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli, who leads the standings after finishing third in Hungary. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-delay.text: BRUSSELS — The EU has delayed a key vote to hike tobacco and nicotine taxes until November to allow extra time for Sweden to form a new government after its national election on Sunday. Stockholm has emerged as the main holdout against the Commission's proposal to raise levies on cigarettes, vapes and other nicotine products. The tax hikes are designed to wean smokers off cancer-causing tobacco while also preventing younger people from taking up addictive nicotine products, which affect brain development in teens and increase cardiovascular risks. Advertisement Advertisement The European Commission proposed increasing levies on cigarettes and setting minimum rates on newer products like vapes, heat-not-burn tobacco and nicotine pouches in July last year. The plan has become a flashpoint for Sweden, which has a long tradition of using snus — a pouch of tobacco that sits between the gums. As such, Stockholm has strongly opposed raising taxes on similar nicotine pouches. Delaying the vote gives extra time for Sweden to appoint a new finance minister and for the capitals to negotiate a way out of the current stalemate. The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the talks, confirmed the vote has been pushed from October to November's ministerial meeting. Four diplomats granted anonymity to speak candidly about the sensitive negotiations said the postponement is meant to give Sweden's next government extra time to change its mind. A spokesperson for the Irish presidency said they will "continue[s] to engage bilaterally with the aim of securing unanimous political agreement at the November ECOFIN" meeting of finance ministers. Advertisement Advertisement Pushing for a deal The original plan was to vote on the latest text on Oct. 9 — just over one week after the new Swedish parliament is convened. But negotiations to form a new government in Sweden took one month after the last election in 2022. Given the precedent, the diplomats said there's little chance Sweden will change its mind before Oct. 9, as the outgoing minister has no mandate to make commitments on behalf of the government. "If Sweden's minister says that it doesn't have a mandate to approve the legislation [in October], then it's over," said a senior EU government official. As with all tax files, the so-called Tobacco Taxation Directive requires unanimity. While other countries besides Sweden oppose the legislation for different reasons, Stockholm's resistance is seen as the most serious stumbling block, said two of the EU diplomats with knowledge of the discussions. With elections looming, Swedish politicians across the political spectrum have campaigned against the EU's plan to hike taxes on nicotine pouches. The topic is particularly sensitive in Sweden, where nicotine pouches are firmly embedded in the national culture. "Other countries do not get to decide over our snus," wrote Swedish finance minister Elisabeth Svantesson in June. Advertisement Advertisement Help or harm? The EU executive initially suggested taxing pouches at either 25 percent of the retail price or €71.50 per kilogram. That would mean a steep price increase for consumers in Sweden, where the national levy is only €18.36 euro per kilogram. Sweden counters that its low tax rate should be applied across the bloc, arguing that nicotine pouches have helped drive down the smoking rate. EU government officials will meet on Sep. 14 — the day after the Swedish election — to discuss the details of the latest compromise proposal, which has renewed a long-running debate over the so-called Swedish experience. Supporters of nicotine pouches say the plan to raise taxes limits smokers' ability to access a less harmful product that can help them quit cigarettes. Tobacco and nicotine companies frequently cite Sweden to demonstrate the success of alternative nicotine products like snus and pouches as a smoking cessation tool. Snus is illegal in all EU countries except Sweden, which won an exemption when it joined the EU. The proportion of Swedes who smoke daily has fallen dramatically from just over 30 percent in 1980 to 5 percent in 2024. Advertisement Advertisement Up until the current government, there was “no acceptance of a harm reduction or harm minimisation approach,” said Karl Fagerström, a researcher on tobacco and nicotine who has received consulting fees from tobacco companies. He said he was not against taxes on nicotine pouches as long as the levies on cigarettes are higher. However, the Public Health Agency of Sweden, an arm of the government, pointed to tobacco control policies including bans on tobacco advertising, tax regulation, age limits and smoking bans for how Sweden achieved its low smoking rates. “The decline in cigarette use has been going on for a long time, and to date, there is no scientific evidence that recent changes in the use of snus and nicotine pouches have contributed to this decline,” said the agency in a statement. Anti-smoking campaigner Helen Stjerna, secretary-general of the non-profit A Non Smoking Generation, said the government’s position was a “tragedy” given Sweden’s historically strong stance on tobacco control. “We’re really going backward. All these things we've been doing for decades, it’s all forgotten,” she said. The issue is also controversial across the bloc with EU countries such as France banning nicotine pouches for public health reasons and stirring a diplomatic row with Sweden. The World Health Organization has warned countries not to follow Sweden in its permissive approach toward nicotine pouches. It frames nicotine pouches as an attempt by tobacco companies to create a new generation of nicotine addicts as cigarette sales fall. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/article.text: Return to Homepage Top Stories: Trump targets more news outlets Patrick Clancy interview Warren Buffett steps down Clancy holdout juror Record diesel prices Trump's 'big decision' on Iran White House pulls ICE nominee Disability claims denied Ed Sheeran tour chaos House passes data center bill Criticism has mounted over the management of an Argentina-run university residence in Paris (Kenzo TRIBOUILLARD) Weeks before President Javier Milei visits France, scrutiny has grown around an Argentina-run university residence in Paris supposed to promote peaceful coexistence but which activists say instead restricts lodger freedoms and hosts European far-right figures. Paris city officials have demanded the foreign ministry investigate Argentina House, one of dozens of homes run by foreign nations or French institutions on an international campus in the French capital. The Cite Universitaire campus, or Cite U, was set up after World War I as lodgings for youth to form lasting connections with their peers across the globe. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement But campus sources and former house residents, most speaking anonymously for fear of reprisal, say that the one run by Argentina has gone awry since a Milei appointee, fervent Catholic lawyer Santiago Muzio, became its director in 2024. "The house used to be a space for community, culture, and art. Today it's a space of fear, control, surveillance, cameras," said an Argentine who lived there during the last academic year. Residents told AFP their access to common areas such as the lounge or the outdoor barbecue -- an epicentre for socialising in Argentine culture -- had been restricted. They claimed constant fear drove them to speak in whispers inside the house, with its director frowning on topics such as LGBTQ rights and the forcibly disappeared during Argentina's 1976-83 military rule. Advertisement Advertisement "It's a mini-dictatorship," said another student, who lived there during the same period. - Far-right meetings - As France's far right eyes its best chance yet to win power in presidential elections next year, various reports have emerged of far-right figures holding meetings in its rooms. Two think tanks linked to the far-right in Poland and Hungary in November were in Argentina House to present a plan to dismantle much of the European Union, according to left-wing media outlet Basta! In May, it hosted a meeting against euthanasia in Europe. Neither the residence nor Argentina's ministry of human capital with authority over the site, responded to AFP's repeated requests for comment. Advertisement Advertisement Blandine Sorbe, of the foundation that manages the Cite Universitaire, told AFP she was working to have the issue of the house's management "raised" at a diplomatic level before Milei visits Paris in late September. The Paris city hall has requested French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot's team conduct an investigation in a letter dated July 30 and seen by AFP. Asked about the matter on Tuesday, Barrot responded: "We are currently in talks with the Argentine authorities and their representatives in Paris." - LGBTQ posters torn down - The Cite U hosts around 12,000 students, academics and artists of some 150 nationalities. Advertisement Advertisement Argentina House has, since it opened in 1928, welcomed generations of learners from Argentina and other countries, including Argentine-French novelist Julio Cortazar. These days, students pay between 620 and 1,210 euros a month ($720-1,400) to sleep in one of its 70 to 80 beds. Life at the house, like all others across campus, is supposed to be ruled by the Cite U's "charter of values", which includes respect for human rights and privacy, and prohibits discrimination based on gender or sexual orientation. But, says house director representative Laurent Schneider, Muzio has refused to sign it. He said he could not, "in good conscience," sign a document that recognises gender equality and non-discrimination based on sexual orientation, Schneider said. Advertisement Advertisement A source familiar with the residence said the director had posters defending LGBTQ rights taken down. - 'Political persecution' - But the breaking point, campus sources told AFP, was when under Muzio, the residence in February removed a plaque "in homage to the 30,000 disappeared and victims of state terrorism (1974–1983)", saying it was for construction work. Milei's government says the figure is much lower. Students responded by holding a commemoration in Germany House, and campus authorities put up a similar plaque across the street. Argentine House then did not allow 13 students viewed as against the plaque's removal to remain in dorms during the summer holidays, one of them, an academic researcher called Salvador Calanni, told AFP. Advertisement Advertisement He said it felt like "political persecution". Sorbe said around 10 of those students were rehoused for July and August. When it came to apply for the new academic year, Calanni said he was among 42 people Argentina House rejected in what he says was an opaque admission process. Cite U encourages houses to take in foreign students to encourage mixing, but the director of another house said he could no longer recommend Argentina's halls. https://www.theamericanconservative.com/.text: Foreign Affairs Three Presidents Pitch Their Wars at the UN Trump, Zelensky, and Pezeshkian each gave speeches worthy of reflection. Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Ted Snider Sep 26, 2026 12:01 AM Loading the Elevenlabs Text to Speech AudioNative Player... This week’s UN General Assembly brought attention-grabbing speeches from the presidents of the United States, Ukraine, and Iran. Each speech contained small moments that didn’t make it into the headlines, but deserve attention nonetheless. Let’s start with President Donald Trump’s speech , which swung like a wild pendulum between the ridiculous and the horrifying. Ridiculously, Trump twice referred to the “51-year menace of Iranian terror.” The Islamic Republic of Iran was founded in 1979. Trump also said he would end the war in Ukraine “more quickly than people understand.” Previously he’d promised to get the war resolved on the first day of his presidency. Trump’s speech, however ridiculous, was not funny. It was horrifying. He stood in front of the world’s foremost international organization and threatened to “annihilate the Islamic Republic of Iran and do it quickly” and “drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations.” He defended the theft of Venezuelan oil with the boast that “to the victor belong the spoils.” He said that American pressure will cause Cuba to “fall.” Trump also let slip an accidental truth, admitting that the U.S. raid this January in Venezuela constituted “a war.” At the time of the operation, the legal justification offered by Secretary of State Marco Rubio was that it was not a war but “a law enforcement function” to apprehend the Venezuelan president. Trump promised that he “will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” But it was Trump, in his first term, who walked away from the JCPOA, the agreement that provided the best chance of preventing Iranian acquisition of a nuclear weapon. And it was Trump who authorized attacks on Iran, rather than keeping up the negotiations that might have yielded a lasting deal. Trump also said that “Iran’s goal was to complete their mad dash to a nuclear bomb.” The 2022 U.S. Department of Defense Nuclear Posture Review concluded that “Iran does not today possess a nuclear weapon and we currently believe it is not pursuing one.” That assessment was repeated in the 2025 Annual Threat Assessment , which stated that U.S. intelligence continues to assess “Iran is not building a nuclear weapon.” In March, Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency Rafael Grossi verified that “no evidence” had been found “that Iran is building a nuclear bomb.” And then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard told a Senate Intelligence Committee that since America’s June bombing of Iran, “there has been no effort… to try to rebuild their enrichment capability.” Trump consistently exaggerated America’s military achievements in Iran. He said that Iran’s “missiles and drone manufacturing capacity is almost gone.” But Iran has continued to demonstrate the capacity to strike targets with its ballistic missiles and drones. U.S. intelligence and the military assessed earlier this year that Iran still had at least 60 percent of its missile launchers and 40 percent of its attack drones. And many of the missile stockpiles that were protected deep underground were untouched by the most intense American strikes . American intelligence now reports that Iran has resumed production of ballistic missiles. Meanwhile, the U.S. has burned through dangerous quantities of its most valuable weapons, resulting “in strategic inventory shortfalls.” Trump said that “more oil is flowing” through the Strait of Hormuz “than at any point since the start of the war” and that as many as 37 ships are transiting the strait every day. But the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations group has said “independent monitoring shows significantly fewer commercial vessels are transiting the Strait of Hormuz than figures released by the U.S. military.” Other reports suggest that the number of ships transiting the strait daily has recently dropped below the average of 17. Before the war, that figure was 125. On to the speech by Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky. Zelensky made a number of claims that were misleading. He said that “the Russian army lost 248,964 people on the battlefield in Ukraine in 8 months.” But in fact, it may be the Ukrainian army that has lost around that number, according to both Ukrainian official Kyrylo Budanov—who recently said Ukraine needs 30,000 new soldiers a month “to maintain what we have”—and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who recently said that Kiev told him 27,000 Ukrainian soldiers were being killed or wounded each month. Following the failure of a PR campaign to convince the world that Ukraine has turned the tide, the new campaign to keep Europe on board is reaching a crescendo with warnings that Russia is planning a conventional attack. Zelensky repeated the warning that Russia “constantly threatens Poland and the Baltic States,” that “Russia may go further into Europe, even into NATO territory,” and that “leaders have intelligence showing Russian intentions.” Both claims are dubious. General Alexus Grynkewich, head of U.S. European Command, said over the summer that there is no need for concern about Russia expanding the war by attacking a Baltic country because “Russia is not looking for a conflict” and they wouldn’t “risk” something when they “understand that… they won’t succeed.” Asked in July about the warnings of Russia attacking a Baltic country, Ulf Kristersson, prime minister of nearby Sweden, agreed : “We don’t see any signs of that.” Estonian intelligence likewise assessed that “Russia has no intention of militarily attacking Estonia or any other NATO member state in the coming year” and that “we are likely to reach a similar assessment next year.” Finally, we come to Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian. Among the more notable features of his speech is that he said about the U.S. the kind of thing that Zelensky has accurately said about Russia: that a major power attacked his country “but we did not bend the knee. We did not bow our head.” Subscribe Today Get daily emails in your inbox Perhaps the most important thing about the speech is that Pezeshkian stressed Iran was prepared for a return to negotiations but that it had learned “we need strength, because a people which is unable to defend itself will be trampled upon in today’s world.” While signaling openness to diplomacy, Pezeshkian reiterated that Iran will not give up its right to enrich uranium for civilian nuclear purposes: “No nuclear weapons, and no limitations to peaceful nuclear technology,” he said, adding that “Iran does not seek special treatment” but that holds that nuclear technology should not be "at the exclusive disposal of some, of a handful." Pezeshkian also pointed to the growing momentum toward an inclusive regional security architecture, saying that Tehran has “a deep belief that no one in this region will have security alone. Either we will build it together, or we will have to live under insecurity together.” Iran War Day 223: Oil Prices Spike as Trump Mulls Imminent Attack Andrew Day October 8, 2026 - 8:28 AM Eastern State of the Union: The president said he doesn’t really want a peace deal.
